notes.text: Vision — Or, the visions; the word being here collectively used: the sense is, this is the book of the visions or prophecies. As prophets were called Seers, 1 Sam. ix, 9, so prophecies are called visions, because they were as clearly and certainly represented to the prophets minds, as bodily objects are to mens eyes. Saw - Foresaw and foretold. But he speaks, after the manner of the prophets, of things to come, as if they were either past or present. Judah - Principally, but not exclusively. For he prophecies also concerning Egypt and Babylon, and divers other countries; yet with respect to Judah. The days - ln the time of their reign. Whence it may be gathered, that Isaiah exercised his prophetical office above fifty years altogether.

glossa.text:
*The vision of Isaiah,* etc. There are three kinds of vision: the first bodily, by which we see heaven and earth and things of this sort; the second spiritual, by which we see, as in dreams, the images of men and things of this sort; the third intellectual, which is in the reason, by which we know the Creator, and, the Holy Spirit revealing it, understand anything at all. "To see" is also often put for "to understand": whence we often ask, saying: Seest thou, that is, understandest thou? Prophets too are hence called seers, that is, understanders. This vision Isaiah saw by the Holy Spirit, that is, at his intimation, he understood the things that were to come upon them. Whence at the beginning he does not set down visions as Daniel does, nor does he say what he saw; but at once he says: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth.

((HIER. in Isa., tom. IV)). Not only Isaiah, etc., *as far as* they were not therefore ignorant, according to Montanus, who saw in this way.

((ID., Ibid. )) "Isaiah" is interpreted, etc., *as far as* and when he shall have done all things, he says: *I am an unprofitable servant; what I ought to have done, I have done.* 

*The son of Amos.* ((ID., ibid. )) Amos, the father of Isaiah, is not the third of the twelve Prophets, etc., *as far as* they contend that they were Prophets.

*Upon Judah and Jerusalem.* ((ID., ibid. )) Isaiah principally concerning the two tribes, etc., *as far as* that these things were foretold for the correction of the two tribes.

*The vision of Isaiah,* etc. ((HIER., ibid.)) For Judah, in whom the two tribes are signified, etc., *as far as* of which: *Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, for thy light is come.*

*In the days of Ozias. ((ID., ibid.))* Ozias is himself the man who is also Azarias, etc., *as far as* so that our histories may appear more ancient than those of the Gentiles.

notes.text: Called — All the inhabitants of the earth, from one end to the other: whom he here summons to be witnesses of his proceedings in this solemn judgment, between him and his people, which is here poetically represented. For here is a tribunal erected, the judge coming to it, the witnesses and delinquents summoned, and at last the sentence given.

Zion — The place where he was supposed to reside, and where he would now sit in judgment. The perfection - The most amiable place of the whole world, because, of the presence and worship, and blessing of God. Shined - Hath manifested himself in a glorious manner.

Our God — The prophet speaks this in the persons of the worshippers of God. Though he be our God, yet he will come to execute judgment upon us. Cease - Or delay to sit in judgment. Tempestuous - This is a farther description of that terrible majesty, wherewith God would clothe himself when he came to his tribunal.
Call — To the inhabitants of them, all angels and men, whom he calls in for witnesses of the equity of his proceedings.

Gather — O ye angels, summon and fetch them to my tribunal. Which is poetically spoken, to continue the metaphor, and representation of the judgment. My saints - The Israelites, whom God had chosen and separated them from all the nations of the earth, to be an holy and peculiar people to himself, and they also had solemnly devoted themselves to God; all which aggravated their apostacy. Those - Who have entered into covenant with me, and have ratified that covenant by sacrifice. This seems to be added, to acquaint them with the proper nature, use and end of sacrifices, which were principally appointed to be signs and seals of the covenant made between God and his people; and consequently to convince them of their great mistake in trusting to their outward sacrifices, when they neglected the very life and soul of them, which was the keeping of their covenant with God.

Declare — God will convince the people of his righteousness, and of their own wickedness, by thunders and lightnings, and storms, or other dreadful signs wrought by him in the heavens. Himself - In his own person. God will not now reprove them, by his priests or prophets, but in an extraordinary manner from heaven.

Hear — Having brought in God, as coming to judgment, he now gives an account of the process and sentence of the judge. Testify - I will declare my charge against thee. Thy God - Not only in general, but in a special manner, by that solemn covenant made at Sinai; whereby I avouched thee to be my peculiar people, and thou didst avouch me to be thy God.
I will not — This is not the principal matter of my charge, that thou hast neglected sacrifices which thou shouldst have offered.

glossa.text: *A psalm of Asaph.* ((HIER.)) *Asaph,* in Latin a congregation; in Greek, a synagogue, which here speaks as faithful, which awaits Christ, through which the unbelieving Jews are the more confuted. ((CASS.)) *Asaph,* about to bring in the voice of God concerning the change of the sacrifices, first treats of both comings, by the first inviting, by the second terrifying. *God of gods.* ((CASS.)) Lest anyone think meanly of the incarnation, etc., *as far as* by way of appellation, as the false gods, Jupiter, Venus. *He hath spoken, and hath called the earth.* ((AUG.)) By himself, by heralds. *From the rising of the sun unto the going down.* ((CASS.)) As if he should say, etc., *as far as: the law shall come forth from Sion, and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem.*
*Out of Sion, the loveliness of his beauty,* etc. ((AUG.)) The comeliness of the Gospel began, etc., *as far as* that they might be witnesses in Jerusalem and in the whole earth.

*Fire shall blaze in his sight and round about him. ((Ibid.))* It shall go before him; let punishment therefore terrify those whom rewards do not invite, etc., *as far as* it shall accompany the wicked to hell. *A mighty tempest. He shall call heaven from above, and the earth.* *Tempesta* ((CASS.)) Not a wind, etc., *as far as* first he called all in common, then he shall call that he may separate. *To judge his people.* ((AUG.)) First he called the mingled from the rising of the sun unto the going down, but then that he may separate.

*Gather ye together his saints unto him. ((Ibid.))* The Prophet seeing things to come, etc., *as far as* it is said of the wicked, *of whom he hath not filled his hand. Who set his covenant above sacrifices. ((Ibid.))*. The New Testament above the Old, etc., *as far as* who hold the works of charity of more worth than the sacrifices of cattle.

*And the heavens shall declare his justice,* etc. ((Ibid.)) Already the heavens have declared to us this justice of God, etc., *as far as* and if now things are mingled, because *God is a just judge.*

*Hear, O my people, etc.* ((CASS.)) The voice of Christ, that, the sacrifices of cattle being left, there may be made a sacrifice of praise. ((AUG.)) Or, he repeats under another word, Hear as Israel, that is, as one seeing God, and *I will testify,* these things, namely, *I am thy God.*

*Thy God.* ((AUG.)) First he says simply: *I am God.* And afterwards he says: *I am thy God.* As if he should say: Even if I am not thy God, yet I am God. For to my own good I am God, but to thy evil I am not thy God. *I am.* ((CASS.)) To be is proper to the Deity. *Hear, O Israel. ((Ibid.))* As if he should say: If thou art Israel, that is, if thou seest me, thou dost not neglect to hear. That God is general, thy God properly.

*But the holocausts.* ((AUG.)) If the soul is inflamed, and seizes the members into its own use, that they may not serve concupiscence: whence it is commanded in Leviticus, that they offer the fat with the little kidneys, by which the inward charity is signified.

notes.text: The definition of faith given in this verse, and exemplified in the various instances following, undoubtedly includes justifying faith, but not directly as justifying. For faith justifies only as it refers to, and depends on, Christ. But here is no mention of him as the object of faith; and in several of the instances that follow, no notice is taken of him or his salvation, but only of temporal blessings obtained by faith. And yet they may all be considered as evidences of the power of justifying faith in Christ, and of its extensive exercise in a course of steady obedience amidst difficulties and dangers of every kind. Now faith is the subsistence of things hoped for, the evidence or conviction of things not seen — Things hoped for are not so extensive as things not seen. The former are only things future and joyful to us; the latter are either future, past, or present, and those either good or evil, whether to us or others. The subsistence of things hoped for - Giving a kind of present subsistence to the good things which God has promised: the divine supernatural evidence exhibited to, the conviction hereby produced in, a believer of things not seen, whether past, future, or spiritual; particularly of God and the things of God.

By it the elders — Our forefathers. This chapter is a kind of summary of the Old Testament, in which the apostle comprises the designs, labours, sojournings, expectations, temptations, martyrdoms of the ancients. The former of them had a long exercise of their patience; the latter suffered shorter but sharper trials. Obtained a good testimony - A most comprehensive word. God gave a testimony, not only of them but to them: and they received his testimony as if it had been the things themselves of which he testified, ver. 4, 5, 39. Hence they also gave testimony to others, and others testified of them.

By faith we understand that the worlds — Heaven and earth and all things in them, visible and invisible. Where made - Formed, fashioned, and finished. By the word - The sole command of God, without any instrument or preceding matter. And as creation is the foundation and specimen of the whole divine economy, so faith in the creation is the foundation and specimen of all faith. So that things which are seen - As the sun, earth, stars. Were made of things which do not appear - Out of the dark, unapparent chaos, Gen. i, 2. And this very chaos was created by the divine power; for before it was thus created it had no existence in nature.

glossa.text: *Now faith is.* Here is the praise and commendation of faith, whose description he sets down. In which he notes three things, namely: what it effects in us, that it is the foundation of all good things, and that it is also of things that appear not. Concerning which it has been more fully said in the Epistle to the Romans: *Faith is the substance of things to be hoped for,* that is, the cause which will one day make the things to be hoped for subsist in us; which is to say: it will make us obtain the good things to come. And faith is properly called *substance,* because it stands under the things to be hoped for, and makes them to be in believers in the other life. And it is the foundation of all good things, which no one can change, and without which there is no good building; or, it already makes the things to be hoped for to be in the heart of the believer. *The evidence,* that is, the certitude of things which appear not, and if anyone doubt of it, the proof, where the resurrection to come is further proved; because so believed the patriarchs, the apostles, and the other saints. Faith is the cause of the things to be hoped for, because it is the cause of the justice through which they are to be hoped for. And this is: *In this a testimony,* of justice, because on account of faith God testified that they were just. *The ancients:* He says this, not that they were ancients in age, but the forerunners of these, and so it is plain that faith is not new, but is to be held, since the ancients held it.
*By faith we understand.* He uses examples for the commendation of faith, to show that faith is of things that appear not.

notes.text: It is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom — How much more food and raiment? And since ye have such an inheritance, regard not your earthly possessions.

Sell what ye have — This is a direction, not given to all the multitude: (much less is it a standing rule for all Christians:) neither to the apostles; for they had nothing to sell, having left all before: but to his other disciples, (mentioned chap. xii, 22, and Acts i, 15, ) especially to the seventy, that they might be free from all worldly entanglements. Matt. vi, 19.

Let your loins be girt — An allusion to the long garments, worn by the eastern nations, which they girded or tucked up about their loins, when they journeyed or were employed in any labour: as also to the lights that servants used to carry at weddings, which were generally in the night.
He will come and serve them — The meaning is, he will show them his love, in the most condescending and tender manner.
The Jews frequently divided the night into three watches, to which our Lord seems here to allude.

glossa.text: *Fear not.* Seek the kingdom, and do not distrust concerning the kingdom; because the Father with a well-pleased goodness will give you the kingdom, not by your own merits. *Little.* Either on account of the comparison with the greater number of the reprobate, or rather on account of the devotion of humility, through which humility the Church grows, through which one comes to the kingdom.

*Sell.* Not only should you not fear that the necessaries of life may be lacking to those who fight for the kingdom's sake, but sell also what you possess for the sake of alms, which is the way to the kingdom, since through it sins are redeemed. Not only share your food with the poor, but sell also your possessions, so that, when all that is yours has once been despised for the Lord's sake, you may afterwards work with the labour of your hands, whence you may live or may give alms. *Give alms.* He who for heaven's sake despises all worldly things, let him sell what he has and distribute it; he who is not of so great virtue, let him give alms out of what he has. *That faileth not.* Temporal things either fail of their own frailty, or, if anything solid remains, such as precious stones, it can be taken away by thieves. But things given for Christ's sake bring an eternal fruit in the heavens.

*For where your treasure is.* Universally, both of money and of all pleasures. The glutton's treasure is his belly, where he has his heart; and so of the rest. For if it is on earth, the heart is below; if in things heavenly, it is fixed in Christ. For it is necessary that where the treasure of love has gone before, there the affection of thought should follow.

*Let your loins be,* etc., *and lamps.* The one without the other does not please God, when a man either does good things while luxury is not yet bridled, or lives chastely without exercising himself in good works. And that you may be able to be drawn away from the love of things temporal, and may do the good things you do with a simple intention of things eternal, gird your loins, that is, bridle the motions of carnal desires, and have your lamps burning, that in your working you may burn with the love of God alone and may offer an example to others.

*Waiting.* Whether you avoid evils or do good, you are cleansed in nothing, but only await the coming of the Redeemer. *When he shall return.* The Lord went to the marriage when, after the resurrection, the new man joined to himself the multitude of angels: from whom he returns when he is made manifest to us through the judgment. Whence too he fitly subjoins concerning those that wait: *That when he cometh, they may open to him immediately.* He does not wish to open to the judge who knocks, who, fearing to see angry the one whom he despised, dreads to go forth from the body. He opens who bears with the judge glad and untroubled, and rejoices at death drawing near; whence it is subjoined: *Blessed are those servants whom, when he cometh,* etc.

*Watching.* He watches who keeps his eyes open in the true light, that he may avoid the darkness of negligence; who also works what he has believed; who is solicitous in the care of the flock committed to him. But what is owed to those that watch he subjoins: *Amen I say to you.*

*And if he shall come in the second,* etc. He calls them watches from the likeness of men keeping guard. In the night of this world we ought always to be solicitous against the enemy, and to await the light that is to come, that is, the coming of the judge. The first watch, therefore, is the guarding of boyhood, the second of youth, the third of old age. But if anyone has neglected to watch in boyhood, let him not despair, but let him come to himself even in youth, or at least at last in old age, because the merciful judge patiently awaits our delays. He, to shake out the sloth of the mind, brings in the likeness of outward condemned men, that by this the soul may be roused to the guarding of itself. Whence, *But this know ye, that if the householder knew.* While the householder knows not, the thief digs through the house, because, while the spirit sleeps from the guarding of itself, unforeseen death bursts into the dwelling of the flesh and drags it to punishments. But he would withstand the thief if he watched, because, taking precaution against the coming of the judge who comes secretly, he would meet him by repenting.
*At what hour you think not, the Son of man will come?* The Lord willed the last hour always to be unknown, that it may always be suspected, and that men may always be prepared for it.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: ‘Enoch… was not found, because God translated him’ retells Gen 5:24, following the Greek (‘transferred’) for the Hebrew ‘God took him.’ The chapter's whole method shows here in miniature — faith demonstrated by retelling the old stories. (Abel and Noah, vv. 4 and 7, are likewise drawn from Genesis 4 and 6–9.)

echoes.text: Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. Yahweh respected Abel and his offering,
echoes.note: ‘Abel offered… a more excellent sacrifice than Cain’ (v. 4) retells Gen 4:3–10 — the LORD's ‘respect’ for Abel's offering is read as the testimony ‘that he was righteous.’ High thematic coherence; the narrative is reused whole rather than cited (Hays, figural reading).

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.”
echoes.note: ‘Being dead, he still speaks’ (v. 4) hears Gen 4:10, where Abel's blood ‘cries from the ground.’ Recurrence clinches it: the same image returns at 12:24 (‘the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel’), so even this faint allusion earns its place.

echoes.text: Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch.
echoes.note: ‘Noah… prepared a ship for the saving of his house’ (v. 7) retells the flood narrative of Gen 6–9. The ‘things not yet seen’ are the warned-of flood; Noah's obedience ‘condemned the world.’ The whole story is reused figurally, not quoted.

echoes.text: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold.
echoes.note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold' is the closest source for 'make for yourselves... a treasure in the heavens that doesn't fail.' The almsgiving-as-imperishable-treasure logic gives high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity;
echoes.note: 'You will be laying up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity' directly follows Tobit's exhortation to give alms. The treasure-stored-by-almsgiving theme is a precise Second-Temple parallel to selling possessions and giving to the needy.

echoes.text: Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:
echoes.note: Ben Sira's fuller counsel to spend silver on a brother and store up almsgiving in the chambers of the Most High undergirds the whole purse-that-does-not-grow-old image. Recurrence within Sirach's treasure theology strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: The kingdom given to the people of the saints of the Most High coheres faintly with 'it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the Kingdom' for the 'little flock.' The granting of the kingdom to a faithful remnant is a coherent but light echo.

echoes.text: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.
echoes.note: The Passover command to eat 'with your waist girded, your sandals on your feet... in haste' supplies 'let your waist be dressed,' the posture of readiness for the Lord's deliverance/coming. The girded-loins idiom for eschatological vigilance is a strong, apt allusion.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' grounds the sudden, unexpected return of the master for whom the servants watch. The Lord-coming-suddenly motif coheres with both the watchful-servants and the thief-in-the-night sayings.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on Elijah; and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
echoes.note: Elijah 'girded up his loins and ran' is a representative instance of the girded-loins idiom for urgent service. It supports the readiness imagery though Exodus 12 is the primary cultic source.

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: The bridegroom-rejoicing imagery of God's eschatological marriage faintly underlies the lord 'returning from the marriage feast.' The wedding-banquet eschatology is a coherent but light echo.

notes.text: After these things — (1.) After that act of generous charity which Abram had done, in rescuing his neighbours, God made him this gracious visit. (2.) After that victory which he had obtained over four kings; lest Abram should be too much elevated with that, God comes to tell him he had better things in store for him. The word of the Lord came unto Abram - That is, God manifested himself to Abram, in a vision - Which supposeth Abram awake, and some sensible token of the presence of the divine glory, saying, Fear not Abram - Abram might fear lest the four kings he had routed, should rally and fall upon him. No, saith God, fear not: fear not their revenge, nor thy neighbour's envy; I will take care of thee. I am thy shield - Or, emphatically, I am a shield to thee, present with thee, actually defending thee. The consideration of this, that God himself is, a shield to his people, to secure them from all destructive evils, a shield ready to them, and a shield round about them, should silence all perplexing fears. And thy exceeding great reward - Not only thy rewarder, but thy reward. God himself is the felicity of holy souls; He is the portion of their inheritance, and their cup.

Behold to me thou hast given no seed — Not only no son, but no seed. If he had had a daughter, from her the promised Messias might have come, who was to be the Seed of the Woman; but he had neither son nor daughter.

And he brought him forth — It seems, early in the morning, and said, look now toward heaven, and tell the stars: so shall thy seed be -

1. So innumerable, for so the stars seem to a common eye. Abram feared he should have no child at all, but God tells him his descendents should be so many as not to be numbered.

2. So illustrious, as the stars of heaven for splendour; for to them pertained the glory, Rom. ix, 4. Abram's seed according to the flesh were like the dust of the earth, Chap. xiii, 16, but his spiritual seed are like the stars of heaven.

And he believed in the Lord — That is, believed the truth of that promise which God had now made him, resting upon the power, and faithfulness of him that made it: see how the apostle magnifies this faith of Abram, and makes it a standing example, Rom. iv, 19-21. He was not weak in faith; he staggered not at the promise: he was strong in faith; he was fully persuaded. The Lord work such a faith in every one of us. And he counted it to him for righteousness - That is, upon the score of this he was accepted of God, and, by faith he obtained witness that he was righteous, Heb. xi, 4. This is urged in the New Testament to prove, that we are justified by faith without the works of the law, Rom. iv, 3,Gal. iii, 6, for Abram was so justified, while he was yet uncircumcised. If Abram, that was so rich in good works, was not justified by them, but by his faith, much less can we. This faith, which was imputed to Abram for righteousness, had newly struggled with unbelief, ver. 2, and coming off, conqueror, it was thus crowned, thus honoured.

glossa.text: « These things therefore being done, » etc., « Fear not. » When the multitude of vices has been triumphed over, the hope of every faithful man is strengthened by the Lord, that it may not waver, but may look for its reward.
« And Abram said. ((HIERON. in Q. Hebr.)) « I go without children, » etc. *as far as* from him, they say, Damascus was both named and founded.

« Look up to heaven, » etc. Above he said: « Thy seed shall be as the sand of the sea, » because in that people some were carnal and earthly, who are compared to sand, since they are dry and unfruitful of good works; others were as shining stars.

((RAB.)) A twofold signification of the promised seed is given. When the stars are shown, it is said to him: « So will I make thy seed, » that is, the Christian nation, whose father thou art to be in faith, namely to glitter with the light of the resurrection. But when the sand is shown, it is said: « So shall thy seed be, » etc., that is, the nation of the Jews shall be numerous, but dry and unfruitful.

notes.text: All men — Although he hath a relation to Israel, yet he hath a general care over all mankind, all whose hearts and ways he observes.

Fashioneth — Having said that God sees and observes all men, he now adds, that he rules and governs them; yea, even the hearts which are most unmanageable, he disposes and inclines according to the counsel of his will. Alike - Or, equally, one as well as another: whether they be Jews or Gentiles, princes or peasants; all are alike subject to his jurisdiction. Their works - Both outward and inward, all the workings of their minds and actions, and all their endeavours and actions.

No king — He instances in these, as the most uncontrollable persons in the world, and most confident of themselves. By which he strongly proves his general proposition, of God's powerful providence over all men. By an host - But only by God's providence, who disposes of victory and success, as he pleases, and that frequently to the weakest side.

An horse — Though he be strong and fit for battle, or for flight, if need requires. And so this is put for all warlike provisions. Vain things - Hebrew. a lie; because it promises that help and safety which it cannot give.

The eye — Whosoever therefore would have safety, must expect it only from the watchful eye, and almighty hand of God. That fear - These are the chief objects of his care and favour. Hope - That place their hope and trust, and happiness, not in any creature, but only in God, and in his mercy and blessings. David praises God for his goodness to himself and others, ver. 1-7. Encourages the righteous to trust in him, ver. 8-10. Exhorts them to fear God and depart from evil, ver. 11-14. God's favour to the righteous and displeasure at the wicked, ver. 15-22 A psalm of David, when he changed his behaviour before Abimelech: who drove him away, and he departed. Title of the psalm. When - A psalm made upon that occasion, though not at that time, when he counterfeited madness. Wherein whether he sinned or not, is matter of dispute; but this is undoubted, that his deliverance deserved this solemn acknowledgment. Abimelech - Called Achish, 1 Sam. xxi, 10. But Abimelech seems to have been the common name of the kings of the Philistines, Gen. xx, 2; xxvi, 1, as Pharaoh was of the Egyptians.

glossa.text: *Blessed is the nation.* ((CASS.)) He calls him blessed who has come to the worship of God: which happens in Christian times, in which the Gentiles are converted, these are the just and the upright whom praise becomes. ((AUG.)) All blessedness is in the mind, etc., *as far as* blessed is the people that has God for its possessor.

*From heaven.* ((AUG.)) From the man Christ. He looked forth in the coming of the Son and saw mercifully, not the sins, ((CASS.)) from which he turns away his face; but he saw all the children of men, that is, all who wish to be born again unto a new life. ((AUG.)) How did he choose? etc., *as far as* he inspired every good will.

*He hath fashioned.* ((AUG.)) He formed them with the hand of grace. *Severally,* giving to single ones certain single things. ((HIER.)) Whence nevertheless the unity of the body, that is, of the Church, may come to be. *Severally,* that is, not out of Adam, as some say that a soul comes from a soul, and he knows them all at once, and all their acts.

*The king is not saved.* Thus are the just made, but neither, once made, are they saved by their own strength. Not only spiritual things are from God, but outward things also. ((HIER.)) No one has anything except from him, because neither the powerful, like a king, nor the strong, etc., *as far as* even if he be in great abundance of strength.

*The horse is deceitful.* ((AUG.)) An animal in whose swiftness or strength trust is put, figuratively, any greatness of the world whereof men are proud: but the higher thou art lifted up upon it, the heavier thou fallest. ((CASS.)) Or, *the horse* is the body of a man, however comely and well formed, yet it is deceitful for bodily health, and for spiritual. ((AUG.)) Or, *the horse* is worldly happiness, which carries men, and while it hurries too much, the horse falls and destroys its rider. *The horse,* human wisdom. *A giant,* someone proud, lifting himself up against God.

*Behold the eyes.* In his own in strength no one is saved, but: Behold whence salvation is, *the eyes,* etc. *The eyes,* the regard of the godhead, which will protect them. *Them that fear him.* ((CASS.)) To fear the Lord and always to hope are joined together.

*That he may deliver,* etc. ((ID.)) These are the two desires of the faithful man: that in the judgment he may be snatched from death, and that here he may be fed with spiritual things, where there is want of them.
*Our soul waiteth for the Lord.* What he thinks of the things aforesaid, as it were a conclusion.

*For in him.* ((AUG.)) Because to those who were absent he sent his name through faith.

*We have hoped.* That we shall come to God, not by our own merits. ((CASS.)) Because in him — lest anyone murmur about patience — he adds the gift, namely that he is glad here in the Lord. And we hope in the name of Christ, whom the Prophet, glad and patient, awaited as one to come: *We have hoped.* It notes a continuous time, because it is not lawful to leave off, whence the weary soul can always be refreshed.

*Let thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us,* etc. He desires that the incarnation be accomplished, that he may be able to be perfect. *In thee.* He says this to the end that every superstition and depravity be shut out.

notes.text: The definition of faith given in this verse, and exemplified in the various instances following, undoubtedly includes justifying faith, but not directly as justifying. For faith justifies only as it refers to, and depends on, Christ. But here is no mention of him as the object of faith; and in several of the instances that follow, no notice is taken of him or his salvation, but only of temporal blessings obtained by faith. And yet they may all be considered as evidences of the power of justifying faith in Christ, and of its extensive exercise in a course of steady obedience amidst difficulties and dangers of every kind. Now faith is the subsistence of things hoped for, the evidence or conviction of things not seen — Things hoped for are not so extensive as things not seen. The former are only things future and joyful to us; the latter are either future, past, or present, and those either good or evil, whether to us or others. The subsistence of things hoped for - Giving a kind of present subsistence to the good things which God has promised: the divine supernatural evidence exhibited to, the conviction hereby produced in, a believer of things not seen, whether past, future, or spiritual; particularly of God and the things of God.

By it the elders — Our forefathers. This chapter is a kind of summary of the Old Testament, in which the apostle comprises the designs, labours, sojournings, expectations, temptations, martyrdoms of the ancients. The former of them had a long exercise of their patience; the latter suffered shorter but sharper trials. Obtained a good testimony - A most comprehensive word. God gave a testimony, not only of them but to them: and they received his testimony as if it had been the things themselves of which he testified, ver. 4, 5, 39. Hence they also gave testimony to others, and others testified of them.

By faith we understand that the worlds — Heaven and earth and all things in them, visible and invisible. Where made - Formed, fashioned, and finished. By the word - The sole command of God, without any instrument or preceding matter. And as creation is the foundation and specimen of the whole divine economy, so faith in the creation is the foundation and specimen of all faith. So that things which are seen - As the sun, earth, stars. Were made of things which do not appear - Out of the dark, unapparent chaos, Gen. i, 2. And this very chaos was created by the divine power; for before it was thus created it had no existence in nature.

glossa.text: *Now faith is.* Here is the praise and commendation of faith, whose description he sets down. In which he notes three things, namely: what it effects in us, that it is the foundation of all good things, and that it is also of things that appear not. Concerning which it has been more fully said in the Epistle to the Romans: *Faith is the substance of things to be hoped for,* that is, the cause which will one day make the things to be hoped for subsist in us; which is to say: it will make us obtain the good things to come. And faith is properly called *substance,* because it stands under the things to be hoped for, and makes them to be in believers in the other life. And it is the foundation of all good things, which no one can change, and without which there is no good building; or, it already makes the things to be hoped for to be in the heart of the believer. *The evidence,* that is, the certitude of things which appear not, and if anyone doubt of it, the proof, where the resurrection to come is further proved; because so believed the patriarchs, the apostles, and the other saints. Faith is the cause of the things to be hoped for, because it is the cause of the justice through which they are to be hoped for. And this is: *In this a testimony,* of justice, because on account of faith God testified that they were just. *The ancients:* He says this, not that they were ancients in age, but the forerunners of these, and so it is plain that faith is not new, but is to be held, since the ancients held it.
*By faith we understand.* He uses examples for the commendation of faith, to show that faith is of things that appear not.

notes.text: It is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom — How much more food and raiment? And since ye have such an inheritance, regard not your earthly possessions.

Sell what ye have — This is a direction, not given to all the multitude: (much less is it a standing rule for all Christians:) neither to the apostles; for they had nothing to sell, having left all before: but to his other disciples, (mentioned chap. xii, 22, and Acts i, 15, ) especially to the seventy, that they might be free from all worldly entanglements. Matt. vi, 19.

Let your loins be girt — An allusion to the long garments, worn by the eastern nations, which they girded or tucked up about their loins, when they journeyed or were employed in any labour: as also to the lights that servants used to carry at weddings, which were generally in the night.
He will come and serve them — The meaning is, he will show them his love, in the most condescending and tender manner.
The Jews frequently divided the night into three watches, to which our Lord seems here to allude.

glossa.text: *Fear not.* Seek the kingdom, and do not distrust concerning the kingdom; because the Father with a well-pleased goodness will give you the kingdom, not by your own merits. *Little.* Either on account of the comparison with the greater number of the reprobate, or rather on account of the devotion of humility, through which humility the Church grows, through which one comes to the kingdom.

*Sell.* Not only should you not fear that the necessaries of life may be lacking to those who fight for the kingdom's sake, but sell also what you possess for the sake of alms, which is the way to the kingdom, since through it sins are redeemed. Not only share your food with the poor, but sell also your possessions, so that, when all that is yours has once been despised for the Lord's sake, you may afterwards work with the labour of your hands, whence you may live or may give alms. *Give alms.* He who for heaven's sake despises all worldly things, let him sell what he has and distribute it; he who is not of so great virtue, let him give alms out of what he has. *That faileth not.* Temporal things either fail of their own frailty, or, if anything solid remains, such as precious stones, it can be taken away by thieves. But things given for Christ's sake bring an eternal fruit in the heavens.

*For where your treasure is.* Universally, both of money and of all pleasures. The glutton's treasure is his belly, where he has his heart; and so of the rest. For if it is on earth, the heart is below; if in things heavenly, it is fixed in Christ. For it is necessary that where the treasure of love has gone before, there the affection of thought should follow.

*Let your loins be,* etc., *and lamps.* The one without the other does not please God, when a man either does good things while luxury is not yet bridled, or lives chastely without exercising himself in good works. And that you may be able to be drawn away from the love of things temporal, and may do the good things you do with a simple intention of things eternal, gird your loins, that is, bridle the motions of carnal desires, and have your lamps burning, that in your working you may burn with the love of God alone and may offer an example to others.

*Waiting.* Whether you avoid evils or do good, you are cleansed in nothing, but only await the coming of the Redeemer. *When he shall return.* The Lord went to the marriage when, after the resurrection, the new man joined to himself the multitude of angels: from whom he returns when he is made manifest to us through the judgment. Whence too he fitly subjoins concerning those that wait: *That when he cometh, they may open to him immediately.* He does not wish to open to the judge who knocks, who, fearing to see angry the one whom he despised, dreads to go forth from the body. He opens who bears with the judge glad and untroubled, and rejoices at death drawing near; whence it is subjoined: *Blessed are those servants whom, when he cometh,* etc.

*Watching.* He watches who keeps his eyes open in the true light, that he may avoid the darkness of negligence; who also works what he has believed; who is solicitous in the care of the flock committed to him. But what is owed to those that watch he subjoins: *Amen I say to you.*

*And if he shall come in the second,* etc. He calls them watches from the likeness of men keeping guard. In the night of this world we ought always to be solicitous against the enemy, and to await the light that is to come, that is, the coming of the judge. The first watch, therefore, is the guarding of boyhood, the second of youth, the third of old age. But if anyone has neglected to watch in boyhood, let him not despair, but let him come to himself even in youth, or at least at last in old age, because the merciful judge patiently awaits our delays. He, to shake out the sloth of the mind, brings in the likeness of outward condemned men, that by this the soul may be roused to the guarding of itself. Whence, *But this know ye, that if the householder knew.* While the householder knows not, the thief digs through the house, because, while the spirit sleeps from the guarding of itself, unforeseen death bursts into the dwelling of the flesh and drags it to punishments. But he would withstand the thief if he watched, because, taking precaution against the coming of the judge who comes secretly, he would meet him by repenting.
*At what hour you think not, the Son of man will come?* The Lord willed the last hour always to be unknown, that it may always be suspected, and that men may always be prepared for it.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: ‘Enoch… was not found, because God translated him’ retells Gen 5:24, following the Greek (‘transferred’) for the Hebrew ‘God took him.’ The chapter's whole method shows here in miniature — faith demonstrated by retelling the old stories. (Abel and Noah, vv. 4 and 7, are likewise drawn from Genesis 4 and 6–9.)

echoes.text: Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. Yahweh respected Abel and his offering,
echoes.note: ‘Abel offered… a more excellent sacrifice than Cain’ (v. 4) retells Gen 4:3–10 — the LORD's ‘respect’ for Abel's offering is read as the testimony ‘that he was righteous.’ High thematic coherence; the narrative is reused whole rather than cited (Hays, figural reading).

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.”
echoes.note: ‘Being dead, he still speaks’ (v. 4) hears Gen 4:10, where Abel's blood ‘cries from the ground.’ Recurrence clinches it: the same image returns at 12:24 (‘the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel’), so even this faint allusion earns its place.

echoes.text: Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch.
echoes.note: ‘Noah… prepared a ship for the saving of his house’ (v. 7) retells the flood narrative of Gen 6–9. The ‘things not yet seen’ are the warned-of flood; Noah's obedience ‘condemned the world.’ The whole story is reused figurally, not quoted.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold.
echoes.note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold' is the closest source for 'make for yourselves... a treasure in the heavens that doesn't fail.' The almsgiving-as-imperishable-treasure logic gives high Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity;
echoes.note: 'You will be laying up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity' directly follows Tobit's exhortation to give alms. The treasure-stored-by-almsgiving theme is a precise Second-Temple parallel to selling possessions and giving to the needy.

echoes.text: Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:
echoes.note: Ben Sira's fuller counsel to spend silver on a brother and store up almsgiving in the chambers of the Most High undergirds the whole purse-that-does-not-grow-old image. Recurrence within Sirach's treasure theology strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: The kingdom given to the people of the saints of the Most High coheres faintly with 'it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the Kingdom' for the 'little flock.' The granting of the kingdom to a faithful remnant is a coherent but light echo.

echoes.text: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.
echoes.note: The Passover command to eat 'with your waist girded, your sandals on your feet... in haste' supplies 'let your waist be dressed,' the posture of readiness for the Lord's deliverance/coming. The girded-loins idiom for eschatological vigilance is a strong, apt allusion.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' grounds the sudden, unexpected return of the master for whom the servants watch. The Lord-coming-suddenly motif coheres with both the watchful-servants and the thief-in-the-night sayings.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on Elijah; and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
echoes.note: Elijah 'girded up his loins and ran' is a representative instance of the girded-loins idiom for urgent service. It supports the readiness imagery though Exodus 12 is the primary cultic source.

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: The bridegroom-rejoicing imagery of God's eschatological marriage faintly underlies the lord 'returning from the marriage feast.' The wedding-banquet eschatology is a coherent but light echo.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Do not be afraid, little flock.
It is the Father's good pleasure to give us the kingdom.
Keep your lamps lit and your robes ready, like servants watching for the door.
We are waiting, and our lamps are burning.
By faith Abraham set out, not knowing the way, looking for a city God would build.
We are strangers here, walking toward home.
Come, you watchers, and worship.
Our treasure is in heaven; here our hearts will be. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture a household late at night, lamps trimmed and burning, everyone dressed and listening for the master's knock at the door.
Do not be afraid, little flock.
That is the posture Jesus asks of us — not anxious, but ready, hearts set on the treasure no thief can reach.
Do not be afraid, little flock.
For it is the Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom; sell what binds you, and travel light.
Do not be afraid, little flock.
By faith we are walking like Abraham toward a city we have not yet seen. Keep the lamp burning; the One we wait for is faithful.
Do not be afraid, little flock. Amen.

lines: Keep your lamps lit and watch for the door.
Do not be afraid, little flock.
Your treasure is in heaven; let your heart go there.
Do not be afraid, little flock.
Like Abraham, we walk toward a city unseen.
Do not be afraid, little flock.
Come, you watchers, and worship.
Do not be afraid, little flock. Amen.
